title: 7 Checks Before You Trust a Shilajit Gummy
meta_description: Seven checks for a shilajit gummy habit: read the extract line, separate gummy convenience from resin research, and understand what a missed day means.

items.title: Check the pouch extract line
items.body:
The pouch lists a 10:1 shilajit extract per 2-gummy serving, stated as an equivalent amount of raw material. That extract ratio is the number worth checking on any shilajit label.

A gummy, a capsule and a resin jar can carry the same ratio. Format changes taste and routine, not what the label owes you.

items.title: Trials used resin, not gummies
items.body:
The human trials behind shilajit used a purified extract taken as a capsule, twice daily for weeks or months. None tested a chewable gummy.

So a gummy inherits the extract's evidence only if its own extract line matches what those trials actually dosed.

items.title: Testosterone rose in 90 days
items.body:
In a 90-day placebo-controlled trial, men aged 45 to 55 took purified shilajit twice daily.

Total and free testosterone rose significantly versus placebo. LH and FSH, the signaling hormones upstream of it, stayed steady.

chart.title: Purified shilajit versus placebo
chart.source: Pandit et al., Andrologia 2016. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; healthy men aged 45 to 55.

items.alt: A timed study scene with blurred research sheets, a glass vial and an hourglass on travertine
items.evidence_label: Human RCT · Pandit et al., Andrologia 2016

items.title: Strength held at the higher dose
items.body:
In an 8-week trial of 63 men, a higher daily dose held strength better after a fatigue test than a lower dose or placebo.

The lower dose did not beat placebo. The amount on the extract line, not the word shilajit alone, moved the result.
items.evidence: Human RCT, Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 2019

chart.title: Strength lost after fatigue
chart.source: Keller et al., JISSN 2019. 63 men, 8 weeks; adjusted mean decline in MVIC for the stronger half.

items.alt: A stopwatch, blank research notes and a plain water glass beside a travertine bench
items.evidence_label: Human RCT · Keller et al., JISSN 2019

items.title: Check each herb's own amount
items.body:
This pack also lists ashwagandha, gokshura and black musli. Each herb needs its own trial, at its own dose, to count as evidence.

A 60-day RCT of ashwagandha alone, taken twice daily, lowered stress scores. That trial says nothing about shilajit, or about this blend.
items.evidence: Human RCT, Indian Journal of Psychological Medicine 2012
items.alt: Dried botanical roots and a blank ingredient card beside a pencil on linen
items.evidence_label: Human RCT, ashwagandha only · Chandrasekhar et al., 2012

items.title: No trial tested a shilajit gummy
items.body:
We searched the literature for a published human trial of a shilajit gummy, or of this exact seven-ingredient blend. We found none.

That is a gap, not proof the format fails. It means the blend's case rests on each separate ingredient's own research.

items.title: A missed day changes the evidence
items.body:
Every trial above dosed people daily for 8 to 13 weeks. A missed day is not in that evidence; consistency is the variable the researchers controlled for.

A 2008 lab survey of Ayurvedic products found metal contamination in 20.7 percent of samples bought online, a reminder to ask any seller for batch testing.
items.evidence: Study-design pattern plus product-testing study, JAMA 2008
items.alt: A blank notebook, stopwatch and clear water glass on a calm morning counter
items.evidence_label: Consistency and testing · Saper et al., JAMA 2008

bridge.title: Convenience is part of consistency
bridge.body:
Format decides whether the routine survives a busy week. A pouch of gummies travels and chews in seconds; a jar of resin needs a spoon, warm water and a few extra minutes.

Neither format has its own human trial. Choosing one is a convenience call, not an evidence call, so read the extract line before you decide.
